symptoms: Small dark spots form first on the older leaves near the ground.
Leaf spots are round and brown and can grow up to half an inch across.
Badly infected leaves turn brown and may fall off or cling dead to the stem.
Fruit spots are leathery and black, usually near the stem.
treatment: Prune off infected leaves if the disease is caught early, removing no more than a third of the plant's leaves, and dispose of them far from the tomato area.
Wash and sanitise tools after touching infected plants.
If a fungicide is needed, apply it when the weather favours the disease and alternate between chemical families so the fungus does not become insensitive.
prevention: Grow early blight resistant varieties and use disease-free seed.
Mulch the soil and water with drip irrigation to keep the leaves dry.
Stake, trellis and space plants so air can move through them, and prune the bottom leaves to avoid soil splash.
Remove or bury infected plants at the end of the season.
Rotate crops: do not plant tomatoes in the same place for at least two years.
tomato___Early_blight.severity: Can severely limit yield on susceptible varieties.

sources.title: Early blight in tomato and potato, University of Minnesota Extension

symptoms: Large dark brown blotches with a green-grey edge appear on leaves and are not held in by the leaf veins.
The infection moves through leaflets and leaf stalks, leaving large sections of dry brown foliage.
On fruit, firm dark brown circular spots cover large areas and may turn mushy.
In cool wet weather whole fields turn brown and wilted, as if hit by frost.
treatment: Check plants regularly and remove diseased leaves.
If only a few plants are infected, remove and destroy them so the disease does not spread through the field.
Fungicides must be ones that work on water molds, and they work only when applied before infection.
Rotate or tank-mix fungicide groups to avoid resistance.
prevention: Plant where no tomato, potato, pepper or eggplant has grown for the past 3 to 4 years.
Keep leaves dry: use drip irrigation or a soaker hose and water in the morning.
Inspect transplants for late blight before planting.
Control volunteer potato plants, which can carry the disease from infected tubers.
Remove or bury plants at the end of the season.
tomato___Late_blight.severity: Can cause total crop failure if left untreated. It favours cool (60 to 70 °F), damp weather; long hot dry spells can stop its spread.

sources.title: Late blight of tomato and potato, University of Minnesota Extension

symptoms: Water-soaked areas develop on older leaves.
Leaf spots turn from yellow or light green to dark brown or black.
Seedlings can lose most of their leaves.
Spots on young fruit enlarge and turn scabby.
treatment: Apply a copper-containing bactericide at the first sign of disease and repeat every 10 to 14 days in warm, moist conditions.
Combining copper with mancozeb improves control.
Copper only protects healthy tissue, so it must be on the plant before infection occurs.
prevention: Use pathogen-free seed and disease-free transplants.
Avoid sprinkler irrigation.
Do not keep cull piles near the crop.
Rotate with crops that are not hosts.

sources.title: Bacterial Spot, Tomato Pest Management Guidelines, UC Statewide IPM Program

symptoms: Separate yellow spots form on the upper side of leaves.
Olive-green to brown velvety mold grows on the underside of the leaf below the spots.
Infected blossoms turn black and fall off.
Fruit infection starts as a smooth black irregular area at the stem end.
treatment: Fungicides work only if applied before infection; follow the label.
Alternate between chemical families to avoid resistance.
Copper-based products can be used in organic production.
prevention: Use drip irrigation and avoid wetting the leaves.
Space, prune and stake plants to increase air movement.
Remove crop residue after the season.
Clean greenhouse or tunnel walls at the end of the season.
tomato___Leaf_mold.severity: Usually a problem only in greenhouse and high-tunnel tomatoes, where humidity is higher.

sources.title: Tomato leaf mold, University of Minnesota Extension

symptoms: Small circular tan to grey spots, under an eighth of an inch, develop on the lower leaves and stems.
Spots have a dark brown edge with a yellow halo around them.
Spots merge as the disease progresses and whole leaves become blighted.
treatment: Remove affected leaves to slow the spread, but do not strip too many leaves.
Fungicides such as chlorothalonil, copper or mancozeb are protective and should be applied before symptoms appear.
prevention: Rotate away from tomato for 2 or more years.
Control weeds such as horsenettle.
Remove crop debris from the planting area.
Stake plants to improve air circulation and reduce moisture on the leaves.
Mulch to keep leaves from touching the soil.

sources.title: Septoria Leaf Spot of Tomato, NC State Extension Publications

tomato___Mosaic_virus.cause: Virus (tomato mosaic virus or tobacco mosaic virus), spread on hands and tools
symptoms: Leaves are mottled light and dark green.
Leaves may be curled, malformed or smaller than normal.
Plants infected early may be yellow and stunted overall.
treatment: There is no cure for plant viruses; act to stop the spread.
Pull up suspected plants completely, roots included, and burn them. Do not compost them.
Disinfect tools and wash hands after working with diseased plants; soaking tools for 1 minute in 1 part germicidal bleach to 9 parts water is highly effective.
Work with healthy plants before diseased ones, and keep separate tools for the diseased area.
prevention: Grow resistant varieties where they are available.
Do not smoke or chew tobacco near the plants, and wash hands after using tobacco: tobacco products can carry these viruses.
Clean hands and tools regularly.
At the end of the season, burn or bury all plants from the diseased area and disinfect stakes, ties and wires.

sources.title: Tomato viruses, University of Minnesota Extension

tomato___Yellow_leaf_curl_virus.cause: Virus (tomato yellow leaf curl virus), spread by Bemisia whiteflies and on infected plants
symptoms: Plants are stunted and grow upright with a bushy look because the stem sections are short.
Leaves are small, curl upward, and are crumpled and yellowed.
Flowers commonly fall off and fruit production drops sharply.
treatment: Pull out and destroy diseased plants while only a few are infected.
Manage whiteflies during the growing season.
Remove old crop residue and volunteer plants after the season.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties.
Use virus-free and whitefly-free transplants, and do not bring transplants from infected areas.
Do not plant new fields next to older infected ones.
Cover plants with fine mesh to keep whiteflies off.
Keep weeds down around the field.
tomato___Yellow_leaf_curl_virus.severity: Losses of 100% are possible in heavily infected fields.

sources.title: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl, Tomato Pest Management Guidelines, UC Statewide IPM Program

tomato___Spider_mites.cause: Pest (twospotted spider mite), which feeds on plant sap
symptoms: Leaves show tiny white or yellow spots and look stippled or mottled.
Heavy feeding makes plants look bronzed or bleached, and leaves may drop.
Fine webbing is a sign of infestation.
treatment: Knock mites and webbing off with a strong spray of water.
Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil (such as neem oil) works only on direct contact and may need repeating.
Avoid long-lasting insecticides such as bifenthrin and permethrin: they kill the natural enemies that keep mites in check.
prevention: Check plants every 3 to 5 days, especially in dry weather.
Water plants adequately and avoid drought stress.
Mulch to conserve soil moisture.
Do not fertilise during drought.

sources.title: Twospotted spider mites in home gardens, University of Minnesota Extension
